By analyzing samples from an exact distribution and using a statistical approach called the Chi-squared test, we evaluate the hypothesis that the graph follows a Poisson distribution characteristic of large-scale networks. If this hypothesis is validated, we estimate the network size based on the ratio of specific walk statistics. This proposed algorithm is shown to be efficient and robust, capable of operating in networks with any doubling property and capable of handling up to N^(1-d) faulty nodes, where d represents a minimum degree of the network's nodes.

We've developed a novel approach to generate initial data for numerical relativity simulations by using the 1+1 Lorentzian geometry of General Relativity, even in situations where matter is present. Typically, generating initial data requires a semi-classical approximation, but our method allows for a more comprehensive description of both spacetime and matter. However, this comes with the challenge of defining the Hamiltonian constraint in the presence of free data, which is typically resolved using perturbative methods. In contrast, our approach avoids these perturbative methods and instead uses a more direct formulation of the constraint. While this typically results in a quadratic equation for the Lagrange multiplier, our modified constraint instead becomes linear, which simplifies the process significantly.

The JUNO experiment will employ a large, 20-odd-inch photomultiplier mixture of low-background, refractive PMTs from leading manufacturers to detect neutrino oscillations. Accurate weighing of 770 Neutrino-Observation PMTs from three major manufacturers is crucial for the experiment's reactor neutrino detection setup. A customized, high-precision mechanical system was used to measure the mass of each PMT model at the Jiangmen University of Science and Technology laboratory. The measured mass of each PMT model was then compared with the manufacturer's designated values, and the overall error rate was calculated.

Time series forecasting is a fundamental challenge with far-reaching applications in various fields such as finance, energy and transportation. Given the complex nature of time series data, predicting future values is often non-trivial. The emergence of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) has significantly improved time series forecasting outcomes by incorporating spatial relationships among different time series. Nonetheless, the efficacy of GCNs depends on the accurate formulation of the adjacency matrix, which can significantly impact the model's performance. In this paper, we propose an adaptive graph convolutional network structure for multidimensional time series forecasting, where the underlying graph is dynamically learned from the data itself. By leveraging the auto-correlation properties of the datasets, our method enables the creation of a node-weighted and directionally-oriented graph, capturing both forward and reverse temporal dependencies between different time series. The empirical evaluations on 13 real-world datasets from various domains reveal that our proposed framework outperforms 13 competing methods, including single-time series and multi-time series forecasting approaches, in terms of mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error.

This research paper presents a thorough examination of characterizing atmospheric variation models used in on-sky observations, which are crucial for analyzing data collected by ground-based telescopes. These models are essential for identifying and removing the atmospheric signal in search of exoplanets or other temporal changes in astronomical targets. We evaluated and compared multiple atmospheric variation models, including empirical and analytical methods, by applying them to real-life data of a planet-hosting star and a control star. Our goal is to determine which model is most effective at removing the atmospheric signal and minimizing residual errors, which will inform the analysis of future Extremely Large Telescopes.

We address the challenge of labeled data distillation, where we efficiently transfer knowledge from multiple teachers to a single student model. Our approach modifies the loss function to prioritize demonstration of specific skills, by assigning greater weight to student predictions on certain data samples. This is achieved through the use of soft labels, derived from hard labels via a logarithmic average of individual teacher forecasts. This logarithmic average was found to outperform both hard and soft ensemble methods on the target dataset, and also to effectively capture the behaviors of multiple teachers on a given dataset. Moreover, experiments on multiple benchmark datasets reveal that distillation utilizing our proposed method yields superior results compared to the existing mean squared error and multi task loss methods.

To verify the existence of ultralight bosonic dark matter, researchers are developing novel experimental methods. A proposed experiment involves creating a monolayer of superconductors with carefully designed holes of various sizes to trigger a quantum transition and produce a signal when dark matter passes through it. The induced signal will vary with frequency and amplitudes will be recorded for each hole size. A specific statistical analysis, called likelihood-based analysis, can compare the data with theoretical predictions and help rule out or confirm the dark matter hypothesis. The goal is to distinguish between dark matter-induced signals and pure background noise, with the ultimate goal of providing precise dark matter mass measurements.

A key problem in sparse recovery, the Basis Pursuit, aims to reconstruct an original signal by identifying the most relevant components within an overcomplete dictionary. The continuous version of this problem, referred to as the BP-Cont, is analyzed in this research, which generalizes the standard Basis Pursuit through vector differences. A necessary and sufficient condition, rooted in a mathematical concept known as "index continuity," is established to determine uniqueness of solutions for BP-Cont, and this framework is further applied to dictionaries comprising independent random functions and deterministic structured dictionaries with a specific, well-ordered property.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring programmable switches, with an expanding range of vendors supporting P4 implementation across various hardware platforms. Due to the closure under composition and hardware agnosticism of P4, compiling it directly to hardware or VTables is challenging, making it necessary to compile P4 programs into a compatible, hardware-independent form. Our research focuses on compiling P4 programs to a novel instruction set tailored to configurable match-action tables, allowing for efficient and portable P4 program deployment across different hardware and VTable-based platforms.

A vector transport equation is analyzed on a 2D space with curved boundaries, 
under conditions that ensure it meets certain regularity standards. The equation's 
evolution operator can be represented by the negative of a second-order diffusion 
operator and is considered to be stiff. A numerical solution is developed using 
the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas finite elements, which involves 
discretizing the transport equation. Although this approach produces an 
approximately consistent scheme, it has a negative non-stiff component and a 
stiff component that has a higher order of discretisation error. To improve the 
overall order of the stiff component, an approximately consistent, positively 
bounded error is introduced through post-processing. This involves adjusting the 
velocity component in a specific set of points and has been extensively tested 
with both exact and approximate solutions.

The growing concern about data protection in machine learning has led to the emergence of Federated Learning as a key strategy, enabling secure and private model training across distributed data sources while preserving source anonymity. This research builds upon FL by investigating the disparities in the learning process and data utilization, highlighting the contradictions between fairness and data privacy. A case study is presented, examining the impact of source importance and data quantity on the training outcome under DP-based FL frameworks. The results reveal that the anxiety about privacy can, paradoxically, exacerbate fairness issues, and that the weight of data in the learning model is inversely related to the quantity of a user's data.

Researchers analyzing data from the Belle experiment discovered an anomaly in $B_c^+ \to p \bar{K}^0 \mu^+\nu_\mu$ decay rates that cannot be fully explained by existing $1/2^-$ $B_c^+$ state contributions. To account for the discrepancy, introduction of a $1/2^+$ excited $B_c^+$ state as a intermediate, which partially transitions to the $1/2^-$ state, is proposed. As a result, first evidence for a $B_c^+$ state with these characteristics is provided. By assuming certain parameters for the excited state, qualitative agreement with observed $B_c^+ \to p \bar{K}^0 \mu^+\nu_\mu$ decay rates and production cross-section in $e^+e^-$ collisions is achieved.

This study introduces an innovative continuous-time Estimator-Plant model, known as CP-EKF, to address random disturbances in nonlinear plant models. These models are based on discrete-time nonlinear equations that incorporate stochastic elements. The proposed CP-EKF method is an extension of the traditional Estimator-Plant model, commonly used in the Kalman-Bucy filter framework, but with continuous-time nonlinear equations. Unlike traditional discrete-time-based EKFs, which apply numerical interpolation to convert continuous-time measurements, the CP-EKF method directly utilizes the continuous nonlinear equations of the plant model. Through the development of a CP-EKF solution, based on Runge-Kutta numerical integration, we can effectively bypass the need for these interpolations and achieve better performance. The article first establishes a general framework for the CP-EKF method, followed by the derivation of a specific CP-EKF algorithm based on the fourth-order Runge-Kutta technique. To validate its effectiveness, the new CP-EKF method is applied to two widely used nonlinear problems: the extended object tracking model and the van der Pol oscillator. The results show that the CP-EKF method offers improved accuracy and a lower computational cost compared to traditional EKF approaches.

Model-parallel training of deep neural networks is a rapidly evolving field, with research advancements creating new challenges and opportunities. Despite the success of techniques like data parallelism and gradient accumulation, issues persist with synchronization costs, such as increased memory usage and communication overhead. This problem is particularly pronounced with large neural networks across multiple GPUs in distributed training setups. To address this, we introduce an innovative approach called Regional Reviewer Training (RRT), an efficient model-parallel training method that minimizes synchronization costs. RRT achieves this by strategically pruning neural networks based on computation and/or memory requirements across multiple GPUs, leading to significant memory savings and reduced communication overhead. Our experiments on popular image classification datasets (CIFAR10 and ImageNet) using the ResNet architecture demonstrate the effectiveness of RRT, resulting in a substantial 72% reduction in memory usage and a notable time-saving of up to 50.9% in training duration, compared to conventional model-parallel training methods.

In three-dimensional chaotic scattering, specifically in the case of the three-dimensional Lorenz model, we investigate how a tiny reduction in dissipation can transform a Wada basin of attraction near a chaotic escape region. This area, where three critical points intersect, exhibits an singular self-intersection and is characterized by an intricate self-avoiding property. As dissipation in the model decreases, the Wada basin transitions into an interlocking region with distinct portions, each of which is associated with separate asymptotic states. This transformation is facilitated by the emergence of complex invariant sets, specifically invariant annuli and rings that separate different escape routes and facilitate the development of self-repelling motions on their boundaries. This process also initiates the creation of non-trivial polycycles via invariant torus breakdowns, and ultimately gives rise to a collection of disconnected escape basins that corral the remaining portion of the attractor.

A specific type of boson, known as the Majoron, is proposed as an explanation for observed variations in the rate at which stars shine. These bosons are expected to interact strongly with neutrinos and could have a significant impact on stellar behavior, particularly in smaller stars. Research suggests that, in larger stars like the Sun, the effect would be minimal, but it's essential to consider as we study stellar spectra and search for patterns that could indicate Majoron presence.

Deep neural networks for video analysis like action identification face difficulties due to the limitations of current video representation methods, which fail to capture key differences in similar actions or obscure video content due to weather, lighting, or other external factors. Our proposed Focus Network, a deep learning architecture for action identification, addresses these challenges by incorporating a hierarchical structure that enables it to focus on relevant parts of the input video and prioritize its internal architecture to effectively process the video features. Our research indicates that the hierarchical Focus Network outperforms existing models in action identification tasks.

This study examines the thermodynamic behavior of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes influenced by a scalar field, analyzing their equilibrium states and fluctuations. Additionally, we investigated the validity of the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis in this scenario. Our findings show that the scalar field's presence can either prevent or fulfill the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis, depending on the black hole's initial charge and scalar field conditions.

This article will examine the concept of stellar formation, a complex process that has been studied for decades but is not yet fully comprehended. Researchers employ a variety of methods to study stellar formation, including both theoretical models and observational evidence. Despite significant progress, there are still many unanswered questions about this process, and this article will explore some of the challenges involved in understanding how stars come into existence.

This paper examines the application of Nested Sampling as a computational technique for determining uncertainty measures, such as density entropies or Bayesian evidence. We will clarify the concept of Nested Sampling, illustrate its algorithmic implementation and the factors influencing its performance, as well as provide a detailed analysis of its numerical outcomes. This research is particularly relevant to theoretical high-energy particle physics, where calculating density entropies is often necessary for evaluating model validity and simplification.

We've developed a general framework for addressing a specific type of Riemann problem in a broad conservation law, especially when it involves variables that change over time and space. This framework applies to solutions that exhibit discontinuous behavior and can be represented by a measure. In doing so, we've established a relationship between the solutions and a particular class of solutions known as rarefaction waves, which we've shown to be continuous and easily calculable. Furthermore, we've identified the conditions under which solutions are stable and have introduced a concept to quantify the solution's 'fragility.' This framework aligns with existing methods for solving certain types of partial differential equations, which often rely on a systematic approach for classifying solutions based on their 'rank.'

Cybersecurity in the "Intelligent World" is a pressing issue, with a particular focus on protecting IoT devices from various types of cyber threats. To address this, there's a growing need for effective DDoS detection systems that can identify common network attacks quickly. Given the diversity of IoT devices and their limitations, a detection system must be adaptable, efficient, and easy to use. This work introduces NBcoded, a novel DDoS detection system that utilizes a unique two-stage approach combining Naive Bayesian and Encoder models to classify attacks. By converting raw IP traffic into binary code and using a Naive Bayesian classifier to analyze the resulting features, NBcoded achieves high accuracy and low computational complexity. This makes it an ideal solution for IoT devices and has key benefits, including rapid attack detection, low resource requirements, and a simple, easy-to-use interface. Experimental results using KDD CUP 99 and DS1 datasets demonstrate the system's high accuracy and low computational complexity, outperforming existing detection systems in these areas.

A subgroup of a finite group is said to have a broad action when its actions induced from automorphisms and non-linear representations encompass a wide range of characters. The present paper examines the universality of this concept by investigating whether every subgroup of a finite group can induce a broad range of characters through its actions, either via automorphisms or non-linear representations. Specifically, we demonstrate that only nilpotent subgroups naturally exhibit a broad action, while we also identify specific non-nilpotent solvable groups whose actions induced from automorphisms and invertible characters cover the entire spectrum, but may fall short of doing so for all non-identity irreducible characters.

This study develops an innovative image processing technique for identifying plant and animal movement in time-lapse videos captured in ecosystems. The proposed framework utilizes a unique feature extraction method utilizing Fourier auto-correlation, followed by a data reduction approach using Principal Component Analysis to optimize image analysis. A customized comparison tool is also designed to streamline the detection process. The research showcases the effectiveness of this algorithm through successful application to tracking the growth patterns of a red maple leaf and a wading bird.

This study introduces an unexplored method to improve the performance and efficiency of modern energy distribution networks.
Notably, our proposed method focuses on optimizing the physical infrastructure of power transmission and distribution systems.
Our approach utilizes a quantum-inspired technique to determine the optimal placement of variable series capacitors and autotransformers in a circuit.
This method also considers the economic implications of capacitor and transformer operations to achieve the best results.
To facilitate a comparative analysis, we simulate our quantum-optimized strategy alongside two traditional design methods on a standard test circuit.
The outcomes clearly demonstrate the superiority of our proposed quantum-optimized approach in reducing power loss over the other two design methods.

This address outlines my theory on how to distill physical laws from experimental data, as long as such laws exhibit consistency across different observations. Inconsistent data, in contrast, may lead to an infinite number of possible physical laws. A recent study on the LHCb particle collision data appeared to yield two conflicting predictions for the CKM matrix unitary matrix, highlighting the risk of inferring an arbitrarily large number of physically nonsensical laws from experimental errors.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider has a comprehensive search for unusual, long-lasting charged particles at a proton-proton collision energy of 13 TeV. Utilizing the complete dataset from the 2015-2018 runs, amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity, the analysis focuses on a distinct signature: large energy loss per unit length accompanied by significant momentum deviation. Following advanced reconstruction techniques, the data is compared to standard model predictions and various alternative scenarios, including W' and Z' long-lived particle hypotheses. As a result, no statistically significant discrepancies with the standard model are found. Consequently, the study sets new limits on the W' (graviweak) and Z' (left-handed, leptoquark, and right-handed) particle lifetimes, ranging from 0.003 pb to 0.003 pb and 0.06 pb to 0.24 pb, respectively, at a 95% confidence level. Furthermore, the research establishes the most up-to-date constraints on the W' (graviweak) and Z' (left-handed, leptoquark, and right-handed) particle lifetimes in a wide spectrum of masses: up to 70 GeV, 30 TeV, 50 TeV, and 70 TeV, respectively.

We have achieved high efficiency in on-chip single-photon generators based on ridge waveguides by addressing two main factors. Firstly, we optimized the excitation of quantum dots through custom-designed mode converters to maximize coupling to the waveguide's fundamental spatial mode. Secondly, we developed a technique for precise spatial filtering of the quantum dots' emission to minimize emission into higher-order modes. Both optimizations were verified through numerical simulations and experimental results. Our research led to a significant enhancement in the overall effectiveness of these single-photon generators, reaching 84% in a specific setup.

The application of neutron scattering has emerged as a crucial tool for analyzing the bosonic transport of charge in materials. Through inelastic neutron scattering, researchers can directly observe the bosonic mode, whereas other methods rely on indirect measurements. This article showcases the instrumental capabilities of neutron scattering by highlighting its role in uncovering the bosonic mode in various semiconductors and superconductors, as well as in doped quantum dots, which serve as miniature bosonic transport systems.

This article presents cutting-edge analytical evaluations of advanced Feynman integrals,
such as six-dimensional finite-volume free-energy corrections, and seven-dimensional
finite-volume chiral condensate corrections, relevant to quantum chromodynamics at
medium strength coupling. These complex integrals are composed of various distinctive
loop topologies and are computed over diverse Euclidean spaces. Our work bridges the
connection between physical and mathematical concerns, highlighting the intricate
connections between integrals and their utility in assessing numerical integration methods
for differential equations in quantum field theory.

In complex systems with multiple ports, certain pathways of energy transfer persist due to optimized energy concentration, even when others are blocked. We've discovered two interconnected principles governing the total amount of absorbed energy across all possible channels in a multi-port system. Firstly, the total absorbed energy never exceeds the maximum amount of energy entering the system, which is limited by its source's power. This finding makes sense from an energy conservation perspective. Secondly, the total absorbed energy is also capped at a power level that represents the system's total internal energy, which is a measure that doesn't change even when energy is absorbed. This second constraint is particularly significant, as it indicates that the system's total absorbed energy is confined by its thermal properties. We've verified these theories through numerical simulations of two different types of systems, one of which involved random reflections and absorption in a square box and another that modelled a multi-fiber junction with controlled light distribution.

We've identified a previously unrecognized spiral feature in the Milky Way galaxy at a distance of 3 kiloparsecs from the center, a discovery made through a study of 13 CO molecules. This finding is supported by a three-dimensional research of the galaxy's center that utilized data from the Large Velocity Gradient method. The 3-kiloparsec arm exhibits a symmetric U-shaped pattern, mirroring the 4-kiloparsec arm in terms of curvature and orientation. Both spiral arms exhibit a linear speed pattern consistent with predictions based on a flared disk model. The mass-to-disk ratio for both spiral density waves remains stable, indicating a constant behavior for both. The mass associated with the mysterious feature in the central region of the galaxy remains unchanged. The gas density in the central region of the galaxy is found to be stable, a finding that is consistent with recent X-ray observations of the galaxy's hot gas.

Our study delves into the optimization of complex functions with multiple optimal solutions.
A novel, variety-preserving multi-objective optimization algorithm was initially developed, yet during our examination, we discovered that this characteristic is neither essential nor sufficient for producing a diverse set of optimal solutions.
Through our analysis, we identified two primary factors contributing to a diverse range of optimal solutions: 1) the presence of multiple objectives, which helps to fragment the search space, and 2) the use of diverse candidate solutions, which facilitate exploration of various regions within the search space.
Consequently, we propose two modifications to existing algorithms: introducing multiple objectives and utilizing diverse parent candidates when transferring genetic information during the optimization process.
Our findings are further substantiated by four distinct test functions, demonstrating that these two factors significantly enhance the likelihood of encountering multiple optimal solutions.

We investigate the roommates problem, a fundamental concept in fair division with clashing preferences. Our research expands on previous work by introducing a new class of preferences and examining the existence of allocations that meet specific fairness and consistency requirements in three-dimensional scenarios.

The valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional group-III monochalcogenide semiconductors plays a significant role, with research still in its initial stages, in contrast to carbon nanotubes and moiraledd transition-metal dichalcogenides, which have been extensively studied. These three types of materials have distinct mechanisms generating valley polarization, which are influenced by the spin-orbit interaction, corrugation, and electron-phonon interaction, respectively. This concept brief focuses on the third mechanism and involves the interaction between electrons and phonons, particularly the coupling between optical phonons and valleys, which can be attributed to the local structural deformity and valley selection rules. This interaction can also result in the formation of valley-longitudinal optical phonon polaritons and valley-exciton phase transitions.

The concept of $\delta$-isometry is fundamental in establishing the cloud of a metric space $X$ by defining the set of all minimal $\delta$-approximations within the space of isometric embeddings from $X$ into another space $Y$, for a given $\delta \geq 0$. The minimal $\delta$-approximations form a subspace of the space of all $\delta$-approximations and by varying $\delta$, the sequence of these subspaces constitutes a nested system of subspaces. In this context, the stable properties of metric spaces $X$ and $Y$ are explored in relation to the completeness of the space of isometric embeddings and its relationship with compact interpolation sets. Furthermore, the concept of a 'hub' space, which serves as a common ground for the clouds of various metric spaces, is introduced and its significance is investigated.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with a broad spatial coverage and wide frequency range is presented. The antenna's unique design features a specially shaped microstrip corporate feeder with multiple parallel elements and a centrally located slot in the radiating patch, which accommodates multiple feeding points. The combination of these design elements achieves a remarkable wide bandwidth of over 28 GHz and a broad spatial coverage with 12 adjacent 5G C-bands, spanning from 25.1 GHz to 43.3 GHz. The antenna's key specifications include a maximum 7.9 dBi gain, a broad beamwidth of up to 114 degrees, and a simple microstrip corporate feeder that facilitates easy integration with backend RF system components. The antenna's exceptional performance makes it an ideal solution for 5G and future mm-wave applications requiring broad spatial coverage and wide frequency ranges.

To build a stable and error-correcting quantum computer, we need to develop quantum algorithms that can correct occasional hardware mistakes. However, current quantum algorithms are typically implemented using straightforward and easy-to-understand classical programming methods, which don't naturally incorporate error prevention. To fix this issue, we propose training quantum algorithms' underlying classical codes using reinforcement learning, even if these codes don't have their own quantum counterparts. By testing our approach on a standard, high-traffic quantum algorithm and a basic quantum circuit, we've shown that the modified codes can effectively prevent and fix faulty data, leading to significantly improved error correction rates.

We present a theoretical model for enhanced metrology in dual-cavity systems with two types of atoms that interact with light in separate cavities, allowing for optimal measurement of time or other external factors. The system's high level of entanglement, achieved through a specific combination of light and atomic states, leads to a significant improvement in precision, exceeding traditional limits as set by the standard quantum limit. The proposed system has the added benefit of being resilient to environmental noise and has the capability to distinguish between multiple external influences.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on a specific type of particle interaction, direct photon-hadron correlations, in various nuclear collisions, including Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and proton$+$proton, at the Brookhaven Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. These collisions were conducted at a 200 GeV beam energy. A detailed analysis of the data has been published, focusing on the direct photon-hadron correlations from Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions. This analysis reports the first measurement of the hadron distribution in photon direction and provides an updated examination of the isolated photon direction. A distinct difference in the hadron yield and angle between Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au is evident, particularly on the away side. A notable increase in the hadron yield and more moderate changes in the hadron angle in Au$+$Au compared to $d$$+$Au collisions is observed. These findings are consistent with the idea that the jet that opposes the direct photon are affected by the medium created in Au$+$Au collisions. A comparison with theoretical model predictions that simulate jet interactions with the medium in Au$+$Au collisions and $d$$+$Au collisions reveals good agreement.

We explore a dual approach to quantum computing that utilizes a combination of digital and analog processing techniques. In digital quantum computing, quantum operations are restricted to a specific set of gates, whereas analog processing eliminates such limitations. Our proposed hybrid method integrates these techniques by initially generating an analog quantum state and then manipulating it with digital operations. A key aspect of our research involves examining the feasibility of emulating fermionic systems using the hybrid dual approach. Fermionic systems are crucial in understanding quantum phenomena and have applications in modeling interactions between particles and: identical fermions, superconductors, and exotic particles. A distinctive characteristic of fermions is the Pauli exclusion principle, which describes how particles occupy specific energy levels. To emulate fermionic systems, we focus on the example of the Lieb-Wu ladder, a well-known model that illustrates the exclusion principle. Our analysis demonstrates that the hybrid dual approach can accurately replicate not only this model but also its distinctive quantum phenomena.

A key issue in machine learning lies between achieving optimal performance and ensuring the predictive capabilities of a model in real-world settings. Various research attempts to address this challenge by investigating multiple features and their respective generalization properties. However, the current methods are hindered by computational limitations and an absence of a standardized framework for evaluating features based on generalization. To address these problems, our proposed framework adopts a feature-centric approach and introduces an efficient, computationally feasible procedure for assessing the generalization potential of multiple features in an optimal solution. Additionally, our framework provides a standardized method for comparing the features present in optimal solutions and those generated through other methods.

This research presents a novel framework that utilizes a single spatial light modulator to create multiple intricate three-dimensional patterns within a 3D volume, where the patterns intersect with each other. The proposed framework leverages a two-step iterative algorithm to fine-tune the patterns and optimize their corresponding wave propagation profiles. By applying the first algorithm, the shapes are refined to match their desired forms, while the second algorithm adjusts their propagation profiles to meet the requirements of high-resolution, high-contrast 3D imaging. The framework was tested using a binary and a phase-only spatial light modulator and demonstrated the simultaneous creation of multiple three-dimensional patterns within a 3D volume, where the patterns were tailored to resonate at specific frequencies.

A monolithic small prototype called CLICTD, utilizing a CMOS-based design, is being developed to test a monolithic large-time projection chamber concept. This prototype involves integrating a time-projection chamber with a CMOS sensor, which serves as both readout system and electrical bias structure. To optimize CLICTD's performance, various sensor thicknesses were tested, along with two different substrate types, deep-submicron and epitaxial, in conjunction with a high voltage application. Test results revealed a break-down voltage of approximately 100V for the deep-submicron substrate and 50V for the epitaxial one. Signal pre-processing and data analysis were also conducted to determine the effective electric field within the high-gain drift region of the sensor. This analysis revealed a uniform electric field of around 1.7 V/cm in the active region but identified a localized area with non-uniform electric field due to the presence of a metalized layer.

A groundbreaking technology called the rapid atmospheric self-coherent camera (RASCAM) is being developed to combat the limitations of conventional imaging in turbulent atmospheres. RASCAM employs an adaptive optics system on a detector plane to eliminate the distortions caused by the atmosphere, allowing it to focus on targets at high speeds. Our study represents the first practical application of RASCAM within an adaptive optics system, having successfully integrated it into the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optures Testbed (SCEATB). Within an area spanning 256x256 pixels, RASCAM achieved sub-pixel-level image registration with an error of less than 0.1-0.2 pixels, at rates of up to 250 Hz. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of RASCAM in facilitating the rapid propagation of light through the atmosphere at high speeds, with potential to contribute to the development of rapid and coherent propagation techniques.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to mitigate the issue of negative interest rates encountered in mathematical finance. Specifically, we propose a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model modified to account for a deterministic jump mechanism, which prevents the state variable from dropping below zero. A key aspect of our solution involves incorporating the concept of fundamental solutions, yielding closed-form expressions for the bond price formula and LIBOR market model volatilities. Moreover, our approach enables the derivate the hedging strategies for basis swaps through the application of a nonlinear PDE, which we have successfully solved in a closed-form manner as well.

Research into the DUNE experiment's capabilities in searching for sterile neutrinos is being carried out. Our investigation specifically focuses on a specific model where a pair of neutrinos, $\nu_s$ and $\nu_l$, mix equally, given the same lepton flavors. We discovered that DUNE's Near Site, using an eight-year proton-on-proton run with $10^{21}$ cm$^2$ of target, or with $6 \times 10^{20}$ cm$^2$ of target and running for 10 years with an on-off neutrino beam, would be able to establish a minimum exclusion limit of $7.1\cdot10^{-15}$ (resp. $3.1\cdot10^{-15}$) for the mixing parameter $\sin^2\theta_s$ at 90% confidence level. Our study also found that DUNE's Far Site would be able to set a minimum exclusion limit of $8.1\cdot10^{-16}$ for the mixing parameter $\sin^2\theta_s$ at 90% confidence level, or with $5.5\cdot10^{20}$ cm$^2$ of target and running for five years in the far site, with a minimum exclusion limit of $3.1\cdot10^{-15}$ for the mixing parameter $\sin^2\theta_s$ at 90% confidence level.

This study introduces novel estimators for calculating mean differences in two-group designs in the presence of both within-group and between-group effects. Our proposed estimators are modifications of the Neyman estimator and are robust to between-group differences. We demonstrate through simulations that these estimators perform well under various scenarios, including those with negligible between-group effects. Furthermore, we apply the estimators in a real-world meta-analysis examining the link between a genetic variation and cancer outcomes.

A novel approach in numerical simulation involves directly resolving interaction between particles through their explicit representation. This method can produce detailed and accurate results but is hindered by complex algorithms that often disregard the inherent physical properties of the collisions they model particles interactions against. In contrast, the present study introduces a new strategy that divides the simulation process into distinct time segments, $m$ steps, to effectively capture the collision process without compromising accuracy. This multi-time-step method can be integrated into existing numerical schemes and, when applied to a specific case of two spheres in collision, demonstrates a significant reduction - often greater than the power to which the grid size is raised to infinity - in steps required to accurately model a collision.

We're investigating the source of radiation produced by particles escaping from a black hole through its event horizon, focusing on quantum entanglement's role. Our analysis reveals that entanglement between emitted particles and the black hole itself is the primary source of radiation, rather than virtual particle pairs creating and annihilating across the event horizon as commonly believed. This understanding is supported by two key points: Firstly, the black hole's entanglement with emitted particles is a necessary condition for their creation. Secondly, the entanglement's associated negative change in black hole entropy directly correlates with the emitted energy. Our findings also imply that the Unruh temperature is not applicable to black holes due to the absence of a temperature-defined equilibrium state.

This study explores the lateral momentum distribution of quarks created in the early stages of high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions, specifically within the framework of the color glass condensate, where nucleons' internal structures overlap. Utilizing the rapidity-Y (or lateral momentum) correlation function, we examine the emergence of a collective effect in the quark matter created in these collisions, particularly at the extreme energies reached in such experiments. Our research reveals that at high collision energies, the collective response is more pronounced in smaller systems, while it diminishes in larger systems, namely those that result in the production of multiple particles. Specifically, this collective behavior is observed in collisions that yield 2-4 particles.

This study presents whole number solutions for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, confirming the validity of two specific sets of whole number solutions proposed by D. W. Cooksan and S. Wang in their research. Additionally, the paper establishes the existence of an infinite number of whole number solutions for the given equation.

When a liquid stream enters a channel with a differing fluid flowing around it, a specific liquid can seep into the main stream, causing disruptions and altering its path. This phenomenon has been studied in various sciences and engineering fields, such as capillary instability and the dynamics of liquid and gas mixtures, and is influenced by the interaction between the two fluids. If there is a presence of surface tension, the interface between them displays complex patterns. This paper aims to examine the hydrodynamic instability of this interface due to variations in flow velocity and the impact of surface tension, using the Navier-Stokes equations, with a focus on the role of shear stress at the interface.

High-performance computing systems' reliability is a pressing concern, particularly in systems designed to withstand failures and ensure the integrity of scientific simulations. In such environments, we focus on improving the reliability of non-volatile storage to protect against crashes, which are a type of failure. Our novel approach integrates a parity-check decoder algorithm into the memory subsystem to detect and correct crashes in non-volatile storage at an early stage. By integrating this algorithm and reconfiguring the way data is written, we have developed an efficient and reliable method to guarantee the reliability of data in high-performance computing systems.

In our research, we examine the challenge of identifying distinct patterns or subgraphs within complex network data. Our work differs from typical graph mining in two key ways: Firstly, the networks we analyze are comprised of discrete, labeled entities connected by relationships, as opposed to physical links. Secondly, the data is characterized by a significant imbalance in the size of its resulting subgraphs, leading to a need for efficient subgraph trimming to curb the resulting computational overload. To address these concerns, we stepwise review existing methods for pattern extraction and propose innovative, scalable solutions for specific problems involving the identification of linear structures and dense clusters within our labeled relationship network. To trim large subgraphs, we adapt and introduce variations of the Bron-Kerbosch and depth-first search algorithms, along with a new approach utilizing subgraph isomorphism. To improve performance, we also explore the application of random sampling and pre-filtering using simplified linear structure assessments.

We conducted an extensive examination of the statistical predictions made by Szeidl et al. in 2020 for the three-body problem using high-resolution synthetic forecasts. These predictions are based on analyzing the ejection metric as a Wiener process to estimate the likelihood of a particle being ejected from the system at a specific time. Our research involved comparing these predictions to the outcomes of simulated runs for equal-mass scenarios, with and without accounting for conservation laws, under zero angular momentum conditions. We found that the predicted probabilities generally align with the actual ejections, both in terms of timing and likelihood, in the case where conservation laws apply. However, the predicted probabilities for events where conservation laws are violated differ significantly from the actual ejections.

The production of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons is studied in PbPb collisions at 5.02 TeV through the measurement of their nuclear modification factors. The $J/\psi$ findings reveal a substantial reduction in centrality-dependent forward and backward coverage, with the prompt $J/\psi$ yield in the most central events experiencing a 67% decrease compared to peripheral collisions. The $\psi(2S)$ analysis shows a greater suppression, with a 77% reduction in central events. The $J/\psi$ suppression is then dissected into contribution from different initial states utilizing a nuclear modification factor framework that differentiates between collision angles and the number of participating nucleons.

We propose a specific structure for continuous first-order logic, thereby establishing an extension to the existing first-order logic framework. Furthermore, we define a corresponding notion of models for this extended logic and outline an associated proof system, which we term continuous first-order proof system. It can be demonstrated that this proof system is inherently sound and inherently complete.

The rapidly expanding data sector presents companies with daunting challenges, 
mainly stemming from the high cost of storing and processing massive datasets. 
One key area of concern is data integration, specifically the cost of testing, 
which has become a critical obstacle for big data enterprises. To address this, 
we've adapted a high-performance data processing engine to optimize our data 
framework's test case selection process. By leveraging the Unique Value Decomposition 
technique, our approach breaks down the complex test case selection issue into more 
manageable sub-tasks and exploits the inherent parallelism within these tasks. 
As a result, our proposed algorithm achieves significant parallelization, enabling 
efficient and scalable data analysis across entire data sets.

The most severe mental health issue, suicidal behavior, requires a comprehensive approach to understanding the intricate interplay between a person's thoughts and external factors.  By gathering both self-reported and objective data from electronic health records and wearable devices, researchers have found that suicidal thoughts vary significantly in patterns between individuals.  To effectively analyze these complex data sets, researchers have proposed the use of a novel neural network architecture, Deep Suicidal Thoughts Network, which accounts for the unique patterns in suicidal thoughts among individuals and can utilize multiple data sources.  The model's performance has been rigorously evaluated through a simulation of predicting suicidal thoughts in individuals based on their behavioral patterns.  Notably, the researchers have established a new standard benchmark, the Suicidal Thoughts Dataset, which includes data from 1,926 individuals with 10,816 time-stamped entries.  The dataset provides a valuable resource for developing more accurate machine learning models to predict suicidal thoughts and intervene earlier.

Our analysis of observations made by the X-ray Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) reveals that the polarization signal from Cassiopeia A's synchrotron radiation originates primarily in a blast wave. This conclusion is based on data collected during a 4.5-day observation period in June 2020. Both forward and reverse polarization modes in Cassiopeia A show a similar spectral trend, with a gradual decrease in polarization signal as energy increases. This pattern is consistent with theoretical predictions of 6-8% at 6.4 keV, a value that also aligns with previous Rocket measurements. However, our findings for the harder X-ray band are lower than expected from the same model. This discrepancy may be attributed to a varying level of non-thermal components within the blast wave as energy increases. Both regions of the blast wave and Pulsar Wind Nebula within Cassiopeia A were analyzed using IXPE's imaging and polarimetry capabilities.

Estimating the smallest possible number $S$ for a given set of natural numbers $b$ and integers $n \geq 2$ has been an area of interest in combinatorial number theory. Erdos originally proposed this challenge, questioning the lower bound of the expression $S/n-\sqrt{n}$ being greater than some positive constant, with the aim of ultimately proving $S > c \sqrt{n}$ for a suitable $c$. This article presents an alternate proof of Erdos' conjecture, replacing the expression with $S > (1-\lambda_n)\sqrt{n}\,$ where $\lambda_n = 0.5 + O_{\mathbf{e}}(\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}})$.

A new equation of state for dense stellar matter is proposed, incorporating the effects of quark interaction via a strangeness doublet condensed medium. The proposed equation of state is applied to study the sound speed in dense stellar matter and its implications for the behavior of sound waves in compact stars are explored. The maximum mass supported by the equation of state is found to be approximately 3.17 solar masses. The sound speed in dense stellar matter exhibits different mass dependencies in the hadronic phase and the quark phase. In compact stars, the sound speed can vary with mass and radial distance, which may influence their seismic behavior and rotation patterns.

We investigate a two-component system made up of a radiation field and an inertial observer, examining how certain unitary transformations affecting the field influence each other. Specifically, we explore the effects of applying the compass state |$\cal C$($\xi,\zeta$) on the field, where $\xi$ represents squeezing and $\zeta$ represents a phase shift. Our analysis reveals that |$\cal C$($\xi,\zeta$) transforms the Fock space in a complex manner, causing it to shift while also changing its cell structure and ultimately resulting in a new set of eigenstates with distinct quantum numbers.

This paper introduces a novel method for identifying the intricate framework of interfaces in complex multi-phase flows. The proposed approach utilizes a skeletonization technique to derive the skeletal structure of these interfaces, which serves as a precise representation of their intricate geometry. This skeletal structure is further analyzed through the calculation of Euler distances at various points, allowing for the detection and estimation of the size of localized regions. Consequently, this methodology is utilized to characterize microbubbles and their behavior in the context of a study on the formation of iron oxide nanoparticles.

Researchers have discovered that certain viruses exhibit self-rolling behavior upon exiting a host cell, facilitated by the contraction of their outer protein coatings. A novel theoretical model has been developed to investigate the self-rolling mechanism of viruses, specifically those featuring an icosahedral shape and wrapped capsid structure. This model reveals that the rolling motion is governed by two distinct rolling modes, resulting from the elastic deformation of the protein coating and viral core. When the contraction rate exceeds a critical threshold, the viral core becomes separated from the capsid, leading to rolling motion. In contrast, lower contraction rates give rise to twisting of the viral genome. Additionally, the model's findings align with existing electron microscopy observations of certain viruses.

Galaxies with U-shaped warping in groups/clusters exhibit unique characteristics, and a specific subset of these galaxies, known as jellyfish galaxies, can be identified by their extended gas tails. By analyzing a sample of 56 U-type warped galaxies in groups/clusters, a distinct separation between those with U-shaped warping and those with jellyfish morphology became apparent. Jellyfish galaxies with U-shaped warping tend to have longer major axes and higher concentrations of star formation. Using hydrodynamical simulations, a theoretical framework for jellyfish galaxies' formation was developed, and it appears that U-shaped warping can act as an initial indicator, followed by gas loss and subsequent formation of tail-like structures. Observations of the gas content within these galaxies support this theory, and it is found that U-type jellyfish galaxies have lower gas masses and more extended gas distributions compared to spiral galaxies.

This research focuses on a specific type of manifold, denoted by $(M^n, c)$, where $c$ represents a non-flat constant function on $M^N$. We define this constant as $c=\lim_{r\to 0}c(x,r)$, with $c(x,0)=0$ and $\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{r^2}{p_M(x,r)}=1$ in the space of non-negative constant functions on $M^N$. Here, $p_M(x,r)$ satisfies the Weyl-Petersen's mean value formula. We establish that if $(M^n, c)$ complies with certain conditions, including a minimum on the function $c(x,r)$ and a maximum on the function $\frac{r^2}{p_M(x,r)}$, it must be isometric to the standard Euclidean space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if a given manifold meets these criteria within a specific localized area, it too will be isometric to the standard Euclidean space.

We have discovered and characterized a previously unknown infrared vibrational mode associated with a unique low-symmetry phase in three specific boride compounds: $A$Bi$_{2}$. This mode is caused by a "kick" given to the Bi$_2$ dumbbell, which disrupts the normal symmetry in the cubic structure known as the Laves phase. As a result, the normal and this new vibrational mode become coupled, leading to a set of doubly degenerate frequencies instead of a single one. Using inelastic neutron scattering, we have directly observed this new vibrational mode in $A$Bi$_{2}$ and interpreted its behavior through the use of lattice dynamics simulations, which also indicate that the average time the Bi$_2$ atoms stay in the distorted position.

We have developed a method for computing electric and thermal conductivity in non-adiabatic systems using the Kubo formula and Drude model, which can be applied to complex materials with strong electron interactions. This involves converting the time-dependent problem into a static disorder-bond problem. We utilize this approach to calculate the dynamic conductivity and thermal diffusion, as well as the Drude weight for the two-dimensional Hubbard model with non-adibatic two, three, and four-site interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the effective mass associated with the electric conductivity diverges in the strong coupling limit of the 2D Hubbard model with four-site interactions and show that the binding energy related to thermal diffusion can be less than the binding energy related to electric conductivity.

This study leverages cutting-edge direct numerical simulation to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the thermodynamic properties of turbulence at a high level of refinement. In the high-Reynolds-number regime, where viscous forces are negligible, we observe that thermal disturbances maintain the same level of organization as the primary flow structure, rather than becoming increasingly disordered. This discovery validates our theoretical model, which suggests that thermal fluctuations remain coherent within certain flow patterns. Moreover, we find that thermal increments are correlated on the scale of the viscous length, supporting the notion that thermal properties are "frozen" into the primary flow, where they resist dissipation.

Three-dimensional topological insulators exhibiting time-reversal symmetry can be categorized into two distinct types: those with a time-reversal invariant topological phase characterized by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index, and those with a time-reversal invariant topological phase characterized by a $\mathbb{Z}$ index. Recent research has identified a novel geometric magnetoelectric effect that arises when these two types of topological insulators are combined. This phenomenon is analogous to the Witten effect in quantum mechanics and is a direct result of the combined system's non-trivial magnetic flux. By integrating a two-dimensional quantum Hall system with a $\mathbb{Z}$ index into the three-dimensional topological insulators, researchers have discovered that the combined system exhibits a half-integer quantum Hall phase. This finding is supported by a comprehensive theoretical analysis and is substantiated by numerical simulations.

In delayed delay-coupling systems, we have discovered a unique phenomenon where a minor variation in one component can lead to an extremely large fluctuation in another, triggered by the system's time lag. By modulating the time gap, the likelihood and intensity of these extreme events can be manipulated. Notably, we have found that these events can occur more frequently and with even greater amplifications when the time difference is adjusted. When the lag is increased, the system's native limit cycle transitions into a chaotic state, and we have identified the fundamental pattern of these events. Moreover, by controlling the time lag, we can produce extreme event production on demand, allowing the system to distribute delays and produce massive amplifications.

We introduce a random lambda calculus as a random combination of lambda terms generated according to a given probability distribution, and define its type system by developing a corresponding typeable lambda calculus and demonstrating the equivalence of its types with those of the original random lambda calculus. By showing the correspondence between types and the levels of a finite graph representing interaction semantics, we establish a means of interpreting types based on cut-elimination time, and prove that this interpretation is consistent with the original type system.

Although various techniques for extracting design conversation meanings have been created, little attention has been given to determining how accurately these meanings can be implied from the conversation's text. In this research, we examine the conclusion reliability of design conversation extraction techniques, considering multiple extraction methods and forms of conversation representations. Our study also explores the impact of these variables on conclusion reliability and establishes a new benchmark for evaluating extraction techniques called 'ConEx' using a diverse dataset of 304 design conversations.

A speculative cosmological theory is presented where the universe's initial state is described by a holographic vacuum of the Higgs-Goldstone field, condensing into a mixture of dark energy and dark matter. The model adheres to the principles of quantum mechanics, including the phenomenon of retro-causality, as confirmed by recent experiments. The solution for $\Lambda$CDM model originates from a non-singular cosmological solution where the scalar curvature is zero, and the scale factor is proportional to the exponential of the square root of time. In this scenario, gravity emerges when the acceleration of the scale factor surpasses a certain threshold, corresponding to the point at which the universe's acceleration ceased and the acceleration began to slow down. The model also offers a possible explanation for the observed large-scale smoothness of the universe, attributing it to the coherence of the gravitational wave that originated from the onset of gravity, propagating in the near-horizon region of the universe's initial singularity.

Researchers use various optimization techniques to identify local minima on diverse geometric structures, such as surfaces and shapes.  By equating the proximal optimization process with navigating a geodesic on a specific manifold,  we analyze the distance achieved by an excess of exponential rate, $\sqrt{\ln(k)}$,  beyond what was previously understood,  $\Theta(k)$.  This analysis employs two main approaches.  First,  homogenization techniques inspired by PDEs help us comprehend proximal point methods' geometric implications.  Second,  the development of a simplified,  deterministic process,  free of underlying optimization algorithms,  allows us to explore the identified rate's universality.

This paper provides a definition and certain properties of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals in associative rings, along with an illustration of the distinct classes of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals and prime ideals.
